newsitem.title: NORWAY: U.S. wary of "mission creep" for new Bosnia force.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wary of "mission creep" for new Bosnia force.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry cautioned NATO defence ministers on Wednesday against thrusting police duties on any new military force in Bosnia and said Washington was not anxious to send troops after war criminals, U.S. officials said.

The senior officials, who asked not to be identified, said the United States supported Wednesday's move by ministers at a meeting here to begin planning for a new peacekeeping force which might replace the current NATO-led peace implementation force (IFOR) next year.

The United States currently has 15,000 troops in Bosnia as part of the 52,000-member IFOR and is wrestling with whether to take part in any new force next year. Key allies say they would take part only if the United States does.

A senior U.S. defence official told reporters that Perry made clear at the opening session of a two-day ministerial meeting that if the United States took part in a new force, it was not anxious for troops to assume civil tasks such as breaking up fights or overseeing civilian police at every turn.
"We need to find a way to strengthen the international police effort" in Bosnia, said the official.
"I don't think anybody, not just the United States, is anxious...to send a future force to provide a general police function in the country," the official added.

The U.S. officials said that Perry was also cool to calls from some western officials such as German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe to broaden the current IFOR mandate in any new force and to actively hunt down indicted war criminals such as former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and Serb army commander Ratko Mladic.
"I think everybody knows it is important to support the war crimes tribunal, (but) launching individual manhunts is a very different mission," said one official.
"I think it would not be one (mission) that the United States would be prepared to urge on the alliance. That has been our position all during the IFOR period and I don't think it would change."

Western sources at the meeting indicated privately that Germany, Canada, the Netherlands and Turkey had shown interest in expanding the mandate of any new force to include a possible active search for indicated war criminals.

Perry himself told reporters on arrival in Bergen on Tuesday that flat predictions by Ruehe and others that a new peacekeeping force would go to Bosnia after the IFOR mission ends this December were "premature."
His statement mirrored continuing caution on a new Bosnia force by the government of President Bill Clinton ahead of the November 5 U.S. presidential election.

But U.S. Defence Undersecretary for Policy Walter Slocombe told reporters at a briefing late on Wednesday that NATO was moving rapidly and he declined to rule out any decision on a new force before the presidential vote.
"The United States is often in a position of having to make important foreign policy decisions during an election campaign," he told reporters.

"We will make the (Bosnia) decisions determined on a schedule which is determined by when they are ready to be made ... we are not expecting people (in NATO) to hold up decision- making for our election or speed it up for our election," he said.
Slocombe stressed that he expected Perry to report to Congress on the NATO issues and that the legislature would not be left out of the process.

Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov will attend a special Thursday session of the NATO meeting and he and Perry will hold bilateral talks following that special meeting of the NATO and Russian defence chiefs.
